title: Physics: Electromagnetism & Optics
subtitle: Fields, waves, light & the electromagnetic spectrum
methodology: METHODOLOGY · Every entry anchors to a landmark study, paper, clinical case or theoretical text. The hint explains the idea in plain language; the note names the primary publication and flags replication status, effect-size revisions and known controversies. Studies and effects carry a replicability badge — 🟢 robust · 🟡 nuanced or reduced · 🔴 failed or severely contested. Map pins mark the institution where the work was carried out.

categories.label: Theories & Models
categories.subtitle: The frameworks that organise fields, waves, light and the electromagnetic spectrum

entries.label: Coulomb's Law
entries.hint: The electric force between two charged objects is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them — the same inverse-square mathematical pattern Newton had found for gravity a century earlier, but for electric charge instead of mass, and capable of both attraction and repulsion depending on the charges' signs.
entries.note: Coulomb, C.A. de (1785). 'Premier mémoire sur l'électricité et le magnétisme.' Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences, Paris. Coulomb measured the extraordinarily weak electric forces involved using a torsion balance of his own design, a technique Cavendish later adapted to measure gravity itself (see classical-physics::st1); Coulomb's law is now understood as a direct consequence of Maxwell's more general field equations (see th6), rather than an independent fundamental law.

entries.label: Ohm's Law
entries.hint: The current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it and inversely proportional to its resistance — a deceptively simple relationship, V=IR, that turned electrical circuits from a qualitative curiosity into a quantitatively predictable engineering discipline. Ohm derived it from careful, painstaking measurements using thermocouples as a stable voltage source, at a time when reliable, steady electrical sources were still hard to come by.
entries.note: Ohm, G.S. (1827). Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet ['The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically']. Berlin: T.H. Riemann, written while Ohm taught mathematics and physics at a Jesuit gymnasium in Cologne. The work was initially dismissed by the German physics establishment as excessively abstract; Ohm did not receive an appropriate academic post recognising the achievement until 1852, near the end of his life, six years after the Royal Society had already awarded him its Copley Medal.

entries.label: Ampère's Circuital Law
entries.hint: Electric currents produce magnetic fields that circulate around them, and Ampère gave this relationship precise mathematical form: the total magnetic field circulating around any closed loop is directly proportional to the electric current passing through that loop. It let magnetism be treated as a direct, quantifiable consequence of moving electric charge, rather than a separate phenomenon governed by its own independent rules.
entries.note: Ampère, A.M. (1826). 'Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électrodynamiques uniquement déduite de l'expérience.' Paris. Ampère developed the theory with remarkable speed after learning of Ørsted's discovery (see st3), reportedly presenting his first results to the French Academy within a single week; Maxwell later called Ampère 'the Newton of electricity' for the mathematical rigour he brought to a field that had previously been almost entirely qualitative.

entries.label: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
entries.hint: A changing magnetic field passing through a loop of wire induces an electric current in that wire, with the induced voltage proportional to how quickly the magnetic field is changing — the reverse of Ampère's discovery that currents create magnetic fields. The relationship is the direct theoretical basis for every electric generator and transformer ever built, converting mechanical motion into electrical current or shifting voltage between circuits.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1831). 'Experimental Researches in Electricity, First Series.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, at the Royal Institution, London. Faraday, entirely self-taught in mathematics, expressed the law only in careful descriptive and geometric terms; James Clerk Maxwell later gave it its now-standard differential equation form as one of the four Maxwell's equations (see th6).

entries.label: Lenz's Law
entries.hint: An induced electric current always flows in the direction that opposes the change in magnetic field that created it — pushing a magnet into a coil induces a current that generates a magnetic field resisting the magnet's approach, never assisting it. The law is really just energy conservation applied to induction: if induced currents assisted the change instead, they would create energy from nothing.
entries.note: Lenz, H.F.E. (1834). 'Ueber die Bestimmung der Richtung der durch elektrodynamische Vertheilung erregten galvanischen Ströme.' Annalen der Physik und Chemie, 107(31), 483–494, at the Imperial Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg. Lenz's law gives induction its correct directional sign, completing Faraday's law (see th4) into a fully predictive equation rather than one only specifying the induced current's magnitude.

entries.label: Maxwell's Equations
entries.hint: Four compact equations unify electricity and magnetism into a single field theory, describing how electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges and currents, and — crucially — how a changing electric field generates a magnetic field and vice versa, allowing the two fields to sustain and regenerate each other and propagate through empty space as a self-sustaining wave, with no charge or current needed at all once the wave exists.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. (1865). 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 155, 459–512, largely written at Glenlair, Maxwell's family estate near Dumfries, Scotland, after his resignation from King's College London. Oliver Heaviside later condensed Maxwell's original twenty equations in twenty variables into the compact set of four vector equations taught today; Maxwell's kinetic-theory and statistical-mechanics work is covered separately in the classical-physics folio.

entries.label: The Electromagnetic Theory of Light
entries.hint: Calculating the speed at which a disturbance in his proposed electric and magnetic fields would travel, Maxwell found a number that matched the experimentally measured speed of light to within the precision available at the time — and concluded, in a moment often considered one of the great unifications in physics, that light itself must simply be an electromagnetic wave, rather than some separate, unrelated phenomenon.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. (1861–62). 'On Physical Lines of Force.' Philosophical Magazine, written while Maxwell held his professorship at King's College London. Maxwell's own words captured the moment: 'we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena' — a conclusion Hertz's experiments confirmed directly a quarter-century later (see st5).

entries.label: Snell's Law of Refraction
entries.hint: When light passes from one transparent medium into another — air into water, air into glass — it bends by an amount precisely determined by the ratio of the two media's refractive indices, a relationship simple enough to state in one line yet powerful enough to underlie the design of every lens, prism, and optical instrument ever built.
entries.note: Snellius, W. (1621), unpublished manuscript, University of Leiden, rediscovered and published posthumously in the 1650s. Ibn Sahl had already derived an equivalent geometric relationship around 984 CE, unknown in Europe at the time (see st7); René Descartes independently published a version of the law in 1637, leading to a long-running priority dispute — French sources still often call it 'Descartes' law' rather than Snell's.

entries.label: Huygens' Wave Theory of Light
entries.hint: Christiaan Huygens proposed that light travels as a wave through a medium, and that every point on an advancing wavefront can itself be treated as the source of a new tiny secondary wavelet, with the wavefront's new position found by combining all these secondary wavelets together. The construction correctly predicted reflection and refraction from first principles, offering the first serious rival to Newton's competing particle theory of light.
entries.note: Huygens, C. (1678, presented to the French Academy of Sciences), published as Traité de la Lumière (1690), Leiden: Pieter van der Aa, written while Huygens was a founding member of the Académie Royale des Sciences in Paris. Huygens' wave picture was largely eclipsed by Newton's rival corpuscular theory for over a century, due substantially to Newton's towering scientific reputation, until Young's and Fresnel's early nineteenth-century work vindicated it decisively (see st9, st10, db1).

entries.label: Malus's Law of Polarization
entries.hint: Light passed through a polarising filter, then a second filter at an angle to the first, has its intensity reduced according to the square of the cosine of the angle between the two filters' orientations — a precise mathematical rule Étienne-Louis Malus discovered essentially by accident, noticing sunlight reflected off a window pane behaved strangely when viewed through a calcite crystal he happened to be holding.
entries.note: Malus, É.L. (1809). 'Sur une propriété de la lumière réfléchie.' Mémoires de la Société d'Arcueil, Paris. Malus's discovery that ordinary reflected light is partially polarised, alongside his mathematical law for polarised light intensity, gave the first solid evidence that light waves oscillate transversely (side to side) rather than longitudinally (back and forth along the direction of travel), a question that remained genuinely contested for years afterward (see db4).

entries.label: Kirchhoff's Laws of Spectroscopy
entries.hint: A hot, dense object emits light at every wavelength (a continuous spectrum); a hot, low-density gas emits light only at specific, discrete wavelengths characteristic of its chemical elements (an emission spectrum); and a cooler gas in front of a hotter continuous source absorbs light at those exact same specific wavelengths (an absorption spectrum). Kirchhoff's three laws turned spectral lines from a curiosity into a precise chemical fingerprint, readable from light alone.
entries.note: Kirchhoff, G. (1859), developed with Robert Bunsen at the University of Heidelberg, first announced in 'Über die Fraunhoferschen Linien.' Monatsbericht der Königlichen Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin. Kirchhoff and Bunsen used the laws to identify two entirely new chemical elements, caesium and rubidium, by their previously unrecorded spectral lines within a year of the discovery; the same principle later let astronomers determine the chemical composition of stars without ever physically sampling them.

categories.label: Landmark Studies
categories.subtitle: The defining experiments — and exactly what they found

entries.label: Franklin's Kite Experiment
entries.hint: Benjamin Franklin flew a kite with a metal key attached during a thunderstorm, and drew a spark from the key to his knuckle, demonstrating that lightning is an electrical discharge of the same fundamental nature as the static electricity already being studied in laboratories — a genuinely dangerous experiment that killed at least one later attempted replicator.
entries.note: Franklin, B. (1752), described in a letter to Peter Collinson, later published in Franklin's Experiments and Observations on Electricity (1753). Franklin himself left no detailed firsthand account of exactly how the experiment was conducted, and some historians have questioned whether he performed it exactly as popularly depicted or in a safer, less direct form than the famous illustration suggests; Georg Wilhelm Richmann died in 1753 attempting a similar experiment in St. Petersburg, providing grim, unintended proof of the real danger involved.

entries.label: Volta's Voltaic Pile
entries.hint: Alessandro Volta stacked alternating discs of two different metals separated by brine-soaked cloth, and found the resulting pile produced a steady, continuous electric current — the world's first true battery, and the first source of electricity that didn't rely on a single, brief discharge like a spark or a lightning strike. It gave experimenters, for the first time, a reliable, sustained current to work with.
entries.note: Volta, A. (1800). Letter to Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society, 20 March 1800, describing work conducted at the University of Pavia. The invention directly settled a bitter dispute with Luigi Galvani over whether 'animal electricity' resided specifically in living tissue (Galvani's view) or arose from the contact between dissimilar metals themselves (Volta's view, which turned out to be substantially correct); the steady current the pile provided enabled Ørsted's discovery two decades later (see st3).

entries.label: Ørsted's Discovery of Electromagnetism
entries.hint: During a lecture demonstration, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire deflected whenever the current was switched on — the first direct experimental evidence that electricity and magnetism, treated as entirely separate phenomena for two thousand years, were in fact intimately connected, triggering an explosion of theoretical and experimental work across Europe within months.
entries.note: Ørsted, H.C. (1820). 'Experimenta circa effectum conflictus electrici in acum magneticam.' Self-published pamphlet, Copenhagen. Ørsted reportedly noticed the effect somewhat by chance during a lecture rather than through a planned experiment, though he had been actively searching for a connection between electricity and magnetism for years beforehand; news of the discovery reached André-Marie Ampère in Paris within weeks, triggering his rapid mathematical development of the relationship (see th3).

entries.label: Faraday's Induction Ring Experiment
entries.hint: Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire around opposite sides of an iron ring, and found that switching the current on or off in one coil induced a brief current in the other, entirely unconnected coil — direct proof that a changing magnetic field alone, with no direct electrical contact at all, could generate an electric current in a nearby circuit.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1831). Laboratory notebook entry, 29 August 1831, Royal Institution, London, the apparatus now sometimes called Faraday's induction ring. Faraday performed the experiment after a full decade of persistent, largely unsuccessful attempts to detect exactly this kind of effect, having correctly suspected since the early 1820s that if electricity could produce magnetism (as Ørsted had shown), the reverse relationship should also somehow be true.

entries.label: Hertz's Confirmation of Electromagnetic Waves
entries.hint: Heinrich Hertz built a spark-gap transmitter and a separate, unconnected receiver loop across his laboratory, and detected a matching spark jumping across the receiver's gap every time the transmitter fired — direct experimental proof that Maxwell's predicted electromagnetic waves genuinely existed, could be generated and detected at a distance, and travelled at the speed Maxwell's equations predicted.
entries.note: Hertz, H. (1887–88). 'Über sehr schnelle electrische Schwingungen.' Annalen der Physik, 267(7), 421–448, at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. Hertz reportedly considered the discovery of no practical use whatsoever, reputedly remarking that he did not see how these waves could ever be applied — a judgment history dramatically overturned within a decade through Marconi's and others' development of radio (see db8, ap4).

entries.label: Fizeau's Terrestrial Speed-of-Light Measurement
entries.hint: Armand Fizeau measured the speed of light using a rapidly rotating toothed wheel and a mirror placed several kilometres away — timing how fast the wheel had to spin so that light passing out through one gap in the teeth, travelling to the distant mirror and back, would be blocked by the next tooth rather than passing back through the same gap. It was the first successful measurement of light's speed using an entirely earthbound apparatus, rather than relying on astronomical observations.
entries.note: Fizeau, A.H.L. (1849). 'Sur une expérience relative à la vitesse de propagation de la lumière.' Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 29, 90–92, conducted between Suresnes and Montmartre, Paris, over a baseline of roughly 8 kilometres. Fizeau's result, within about 5% of the modern accepted value, gave Maxwell the precise, independently measured figure he needed to compare against his own theoretical calculation of electromagnetic wave speed (see th7).

entries.label: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics
entries.hint: Ibn al-Haytham systematically overturned the ancient Greek assumption that vision worked by rays emitted from the eye, arguing instead — and demonstrating experimentally using a camera obscura — that light travels from illuminated objects into the eye, establishing the basic geometric framework and the experimental, evidence-based methodology optics has followed ever since.
entries.note: Ibn al-Haytham [Alhazen] (c. 1021). Kitāb al-Manāẓir ['Book of Optics'], written in Cairo. Translated into Latin in the twelfth century as De Aspectibus, the work profoundly influenced the later European optical tradition through Roger Bacon, Witelo, and eventually Kepler; Ibn al-Haytham's insistence on testing theoretical claims against controlled experiment, centuries before the term 'scientific method' existed, is now widely credited by historians of science as a genuinely foundational methodological contribution, independent of his specific optical results.

entries.label: Newton's Prism Experiments
entries.hint: Isaac Newton passed a beam of sunlight through a glass prism and showed it split into a full spectrum of colours — then, in his decisive 'experimentum crucis,' isolated a single colour from that spectrum and passed it through a second prism, finding it remained unchanged, proving the colours were already present in white light itself rather than being created by the prism or the glass.
entries.note: Newton, I. (1672). 'A Letter... Containing His New Theory about Light and Colors.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 6(80), 3075–3087, describing experiments largely conducted at Trinity College, Cambridge (with some earlier work at Woolsthorpe during 1665–66, while Cambridge was closed due to plague). The paper triggered an immediate, bruising public dispute with Robert Hooke over priority and interpretation, one of several such disputes that shaped Newton's famously guarded, conflict-averse approach to publishing for much of the rest of his career.

entries.label: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
entries.hint: Thomas Young passed light through two closely spaced narrow slits and observed the resulting pattern on a screen behind them: not two simple bright bands, but a whole series of alternating bright and dark stripes — exactly the interference pattern two overlapping sets of water ripples would produce, and something a stream of Newtonian light particles offered no obvious way to explain at all.
entries.note: Young, T. (1804). 'The Bakerian Lecture: Experiments and Calculations Relative to Physical Optics.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 94, 1–16, delivered at the Royal Institution, London, describing experiments performed from around 1801–03. Young's result was met with fierce, often personally hostile resistance from defenders of Newton's corpuscular theory, particularly reviewer Henry Brougham in the Edinburgh Review; Fresnel's independent, more mathematically complete wave theory over a decade later (see st10) is what ultimately secured the wave picture's acceptance.

entries.label: Fresnel's Diffraction Theory and the Poisson Spot
entries.hint: Augustin-Jean Fresnel submitted a mathematically rigorous wave theory of diffraction to a French Academy prize competition; judge Siméon Poisson, a committed particle-theory partisan, worked through the mathematics and pointed out it made an absurd-sounding prediction — a bright spot exactly at the centre of the shadow cast by a small circular disc — intending it as a decisive objection. François Arago promptly built the apparatus and found the predicted spot exactly where the wave theory said it should be.
entries.note: Fresnel, A.J. (1818). 'Mémoire sur la diffraction de la lumière,' submitted to the French Academy of Sciences prize competition, Paris, with Arago's experimental confirmation performed the same year. The episode, in which an intended objection accidentally became the theory's most dramatic and celebrated confirmation, is now often cited as an example of a genuinely decisive, falsifiable scientific prediction; Fresnel won the prize despite Poisson's initial skepticism.

entries.label: Röntgen's Discovery of X-rays
entries.hint: Wilhelm Röntgen, experimenting with a cathode ray tube wrapped in black cardboard to block visible light, noticed a nearby fluorescent screen still glowed faintly even though no visible light could possibly be reaching it — and traced the effect to a previously unknown, highly penetrating form of invisible radiation he cautiously named 'X-rays,' using 'X' for the unknown, exactly as in an algebra equation.
entries.note: Röntgen, W.C. (1895). 'Über eine neue Art von Strahlen.' Sitzungsberichte der Physikalisch-medizinischen Gesellschaft zu Würzburg, at the University of Würzburg. Röntgen took the first-ever X-ray image of a living human body just weeks later, an eerie photograph of his wife Anna Bertha's hand clearly showing her bones and wedding ring, and became the first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901; he refused to patent the discovery, insisting it should belong freely to humanity.

categories.label: Effects & Phenomena
categories.subtitle: Named, replicable patterns in electromagnetic and optical systems

entries.label: Total Internal Reflection
entries.hint: Light travelling inside a denser medium and striking the boundary with a less dense medium at a steep enough angle reflects entirely back inside, as if the boundary were a perfect mirror, rather than partly refracting through as it normally would. John Tyndall demonstrated the effect vividly by shining light into a curved stream of water flowing from a tank, showing the light stayed trapped inside the water jet, bending around its curve — the direct ancestor of the fibre-optic cable.
entries.note: Tyndall, J. (1870). Public lecture demonstration, Royal Institution, London, popularising an effect first noted by Jean-Daniel Colladon in Geneva in the early 1840s. Total internal reflection only occurs above a specific 'critical angle' set by the two media's refractive indices; below that angle, light still partially refracts through the boundary as usual.

entries.label: The Rainbow
entries.hint: Sunlight entering a raindrop refracts, reflects once off the droplet's inner back surface, and refracts again on its way out, with the exact angle this whole path bends light depending slightly on wavelength — spreading white sunlight into the familiar arc of colours. A fainter, wider secondary rainbow, with its colours reversed, comes from light that reflects twice inside the droplet before emerging.
entries.note: Theodoric of Freiberg (c. 1304). De iride et radialibus impressionibus, written while Theodoric was a Dominican friar in Freiberg. Theodoric correctly worked out the primary and secondary bow's geometry using glass spheres filled with water to model individual raindrops, over three centuries before Descartes' independent 1637 refinement using early calculus-adjacent methods, though Theodoric's work remained largely unknown outside a narrow scholarly circle for centuries.

entries.label: Newton's Rings
entries.hint: Pressing a slightly curved glass lens against a flat glass plate produces a pattern of concentric bright and dark rings, radiating outward from the point of contact — caused by light reflecting off the thin, wedge-shaped air gap between the two glass surfaces and interfering with itself, constructively at some thicknesses and destructively at others.
entries.note: Newton, I. (1704). Opticks. London: Royal Society, Book II — though Robert Hooke had already observed and described the same rings in his 1665 Micrographia. Newton, working within his corpuscular theory of light, could describe the ring pattern mathematically with real precision but never gave a satisfying explanation for why it occurred, a puzzle only properly resolved once the wave theory of light was established over a century later.

entries.label: The Doppler Effect (for Light)
entries.hint: Light from a source moving toward an observer is compressed to shorter, bluer wavelengths, and light from a source moving away is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths — the same pitch-shifting effect a passing ambulance siren produces for sound, but for light. The effect is central to modern astronomy, since a star or galaxy's redshift directly reveals how fast it's moving away from Earth.
entries.note: Doppler, C. (1842). 'Über das farbige Licht der Doppelsterne und einiger anderer Gestirne des Himmels.' Abhandlungen der Königlichen Böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften, Prague. Doppler originally (and incorrectly) proposed the effect as the explanation for why some binary stars appear different colours, a specific claim later shown to be wrong; the general principle itself, refined by Hippolyte Fizeau for light in 1848, proved exactly correct and became foundational to twentieth-century observational cosmology.

entries.label: The Aurora Borealis
entries.hint: Charged particles streaming from the Sun are funnelled by Earth's magnetic field toward the poles, where they collide with atoms high in the atmosphere and make them glow — producing the shifting curtains of green, red, and violet light visible in the polar sky. The specific colours depend on which atmospheric gas is doing the glowing and at what altitude: green and red from oxygen, blue and purple from nitrogen.
entries.note: Birkeland, K. (1908–13). The Norwegian Aurora Polaris Expedition 1902–1903, Christiania. Birkeland built a magnetised sphere ('terrella') in a vacuum chamber and bombarded it with an electron beam, reproducing auroral-like glowing rings around its magnetic poles in miniature; his theory that the aurora is driven by solar particles interacting with Earth's magnetic field was met with considerable skepticism for decades and was only fully vindicated by direct satellite measurements of the solar wind in the 1960s.

entries.label: The Skin Effect
entries.hint: An alternating electric current flowing through a conductor doesn't distribute itself evenly through the wire's whole cross-section — it concentrates increasingly near the outer surface as the frequency rises, leaving the conductor's core carrying almost no current at all at high enough frequencies. The effect means high-frequency wires and cables are often built as thin conductive tubes or braids rather than solid rods, since the unused interior material would be wasted.
entries.note: Rayleigh, Lord (J.W. Strutt) (1886) and Oliver Heaviside (1884–89) independently worked out the mathematical theory, building on Horace Lamb's earlier 1883 analysis of related electromagnetic induction problems, largely developed while Heaviside worked from home in London on telegraph transmission theory. The skin effect sets a hard practical limit on how efficiently high-frequency and radio-frequency currents can be carried through ordinary wire, motivating specialised conductor designs like Litz wire.

entries.label: The Faraday Cage
entries.hint: An enclosure made of conducting material blocks external electric fields from reaching whatever is inside it, because the enclosure's own free charges instantly rearrange themselves to exactly cancel the external field throughout the interior — the same principle that keeps you safe from a lightning strike inside a metal-bodied car, and that shields sensitive electronics from outside electromagnetic interference.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1836). 'Experimental Researches in Electricity, Eleventh Series.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, at the Royal Institution, London — the famous 'ice pail experiment,' in which Faraday showed a charged object lowered into a metal container induces an exactly equal and opposite charge on the container's outside, with the container's interior remaining entirely field-free regardless of the charged object's exact position inside.

entries.label: Fata Morgana and Atmospheric Mirages
entries.hint: Light bends as it passes through air layers of different temperature and density, and under the right conditions — a sharp temperature gradient near the ground or sea surface — this bending can produce dramatically distorted, stretched, or even inverted and stacked images of distant objects, including ships, coastlines, or the horizon itself appearing to float, tower, or duplicate.
entries.note: Monge, G. (1798–99). Described during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, giving one of the first physically grounded scientific explanations of desert mirages as continuous atmospheric refraction rather than any kind of optical illusion originating in the eye or mind. The more elaborate 'Fata Morgana' variant, producing tall, complex, rapidly shifting images, requires a specific temperature-inversion layer and is most commonly seen over polar seas and the Strait of Messina, the location its Italian name (after the sorceress Morgan le Fay) originally referenced.

entries.label: Ionospheric Radio Wave Reflection
entries.hint: Radio waves bounced off a layer of electrically charged particles high in the atmosphere can travel far beyond the visual horizon, reflecting back down to Earth and letting a signal skip across enormous distances — including all the way around the curve of the planet — rather than travelling only in the straight line the wave's geometry alone would suggest.
entries.note: Appleton, E.V. (1924–25). Experimentally confirmed the reflecting layer's existence at King's College London, following Oliver Heaviside's and Arthur Kennelly's independent 1902 theoretical proposals that such a layer must exist to explain Marconi's 1901 transatlantic radio transmission (see db6). Appleton received the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery; the ionosphere's reflectivity varies significantly with solar activity and time of day, a major practical complication for long-distance shortwave radio communication.

categories.label: Key Concepts
categories.subtitle: The building blocks and vocabulary every student must command

entries.label: Electric Field
entries.hint: Rather than treating electric forces as instantaneous action reaching directly across empty space between two charges, the field concept treats every charge as continuously filling the space around it with an invisible electric field, and a second charge placed anywhere in that field simply responds to the field's local strength and direction at its own position — removing the need for any charge to somehow act instantaneously at a distance.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1852). 'On the Physical Character of the Lines of Magnetic Force.' Philosophical Magazine, 4th series, 3(20), 401–428, at the Royal Institution, London. Faraday, without significant formal mathematical training, developed the field picture largely through physical intuition and visualisation; James Clerk Maxwell gave it its full rigorous mathematical form a decade later (see th6), famously crediting Faraday's conceptual groundwork as indispensable to his own theory.

entries.label: Magnetic Field & Field Lines
entries.hint: Sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper held over a magnet, and they arrange themselves into clear curved lines running from one pole to the other — Faraday's 'lines of force,' a direct visualisation of the magnetic field's direction and relative strength at every point in space, dense where the field is strong and sparse where it's weak.
entries.note: Faraday, M. Experimental Researches in Electricity, Series I–III, collected edition (1839), London: Richard and John Edward Taylor. Faraday treated the field lines as physically real, not merely a convenient calculating device — a view many contemporaries, more committed to action-at-a-distance thinking, found difficult to accept; Maxwell's later mathematical formalisation vindicated the physical reality of the field description Faraday had insisted on.

entries.label: Capacitance
entries.hint: Capacitance measures how much electric charge a conductor or pair of conductors can store for a given voltage applied across them — a property depending on the conductors' size, shape, separation, and the material between them, letting devices called capacitors store and release electrical energy rapidly, unlike a battery's comparatively slow chemical charge and discharge.
entries.note: Cavendish, H. (c. 1771, unpublished), only made public in Maxwell, J.C. (Ed.) (1879). The Electrical Researches of the Honourable Henry Cavendish. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Cavendish had privately and systematically measured what he called 'capacity' decades before the concept was formally named or widely used, but left the work entirely unpublished during his lifetime; Maxwell, editing Cavendish's papers a century later, was startled to find Cavendish had already anticipated several results usually credited to much later researchers.

entries.label: Electromagnetic Radiation
entries.hint: Visible light is only a narrow slice of a much broader spectrum of electromagnetic radiation — the same basic phenomenon, an oscillating electric and magnetic field travelling through space, differing only in wavelength, from long radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. William Herschel's discovery of an invisible form of radiation just beyond red light was the first hint that visible light was only part of a much larger picture.
entries.note: Herschel, W. (1800). 'Experiments on the Refrangibility of the Invisible Rays of the Sun.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 90, 284–292, conducted at his home observatory in Slough. Herschel discovered infrared radiation by measuring temperature with thermometers placed at different points beyond the red end of a sunlight spectrum cast by a prism, finding the highest temperature reading fell in a region where no visible light was present at all.

entries.label: Refractive Index
entries.hint: A material's refractive index measures how much slower light travels through it compared to a vacuum, and directly determines how sharply light bends when crossing the material's boundary — a higher refractive index means slower light and sharper bending. Joseph von Fraunhofer used his own newly catalogued dark spectral lines as precise, reproducible reference wavelengths, letting him measure glass refractive indices with unprecedented accuracy for his optical instrument workshop.
entries.note: Fraunhofer, J. von (1817). 'Bestimmung des Brechungs- und des Farbenzerstreungs-Vermögens verschiedener Glasarten.' Denkschriften der Königlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu München, at his optical instrument workshop in Munich. Fraunhofer's precision glass and lens work, directly enabled by these refractive index measurements, made Bavarian optical instruments the finest available anywhere in the world for decades, transforming telescope and microscope manufacturing.

entries.label: Coherence
entries.hint: Two light waves can only reliably interfere with each other — producing a stable, visible pattern of bright and dark bands rather than a rapidly flickering, average blur — if they maintain a fixed, unchanging phase relationship with each other over time, a property called coherence. Ordinary light sources like the Sun or a light bulb emit light incoherently, which is exactly why Young's and Fresnel's experiments had to cleverly split a single beam into two rather than simply combining light from two separate lamps.
entries.note: Fresnel, A.J. & Arago, D.F.J. (1819). 'Mémoire sur l'action que les rayons de lumière polarisée exercent les uns sur les autres.' Annales de Chimie et de Physique, Paris — the 'Fresnel–Arago laws,' establishing exactly when and whether two light beams can interfere. The concept became essential a century later to the operation of the laser (see ap5), whose defining property is that it produces highly coherent light no ordinary source can match.

entries.label: Spectral Lines
entries.hint: Pass sunlight through a sufficiently narrow slit and a prism, and instead of a perfectly smooth rainbow, the spectrum is crossed by hundreds of thin, dark lines at precise, reproducible wavelengths — each one corresponding to light absorbed by a specific chemical element somewhere between the Sun's surface and the observer, a discovery that turned the spectrum itself into a chemical readout.
entries.note: Fraunhofer, J. von (1814–15). 'Bestimmung des Brechungs- und Farben-Zerstreuungsvermögens verschiedener Glasarten.' Denkschriften der Königlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu München, at his workshop in Munich, cataloguing what are now called Fraunhofer lines. Fraunhofer counted and catalogued nearly 600 dark lines without knowing what caused them; Kirchhoff and Bunsen supplied the explanation four decades later (see th11), identifying the lines as absorption fingerprints of specific elements.

entries.label: Impedance
entries.hint: In an alternating-current circuit, resistance alone isn't enough to describe how a component opposes current flow — capacitors and inductors also introduce a frequency-dependent opposition, and a phase shift between voltage and current, that Ohm's simple law alone can't capture. Impedance generalises resistance into a single quantity accounting for all three effects together, letting AC circuits be analysed using much the same algebraic tools Ohm's law provides for simple DC circuits.
entries.note: Heaviside, O. (1886–89). 'Electromagnetic Induction and Its Propagation.' The Electrician, developed largely in isolation while Heaviside worked unpaid and without an academic position, supporting himself on a small income while living with relatives in Devon. Heaviside's operational calculus and impedance concept were initially dismissed by parts of the physics establishment as mathematically unrigorous, though they proved immensely practically useful and were later given a fully rigorous footing.

entries.label: Polarization
entries.hint: Ordinary light vibrates in every direction perpendicular to its direction of travel; polarised light has had all but one specific vibration direction filtered out. Erasmus Bartholin discovered the phenomenon's first clear signature — double refraction — by looking through a clear crystal of Iceland spar and finding it split a single beam of light into two separate, distinctly behaving beams, over a century before anyone understood why.
entries.note: Bartholin, E. (1669). Experimenta crystalli islandici disdiaclastici. Copenhagen, describing calcite's unusual double-refraction property. Huygens (1690, see th9) offered a partial wave-based explanation for the two beams' different behaviour; the full picture, that the two beams are polarised at right angles to each other, was only established by Malus's and Fresnel's work well over a century later (see th10).

categories.label: Methods & Approaches
categories.subtitle: The tools and paradigms that generate the field's evidence

entries.label: The Wheatstone Bridge
entries.hint: To measure an unknown electrical resistance with high precision, arrange it in a diamond-shaped circuit alongside three known resistances, and adjust one of the known values until a sensitive galvanometer bridging the circuit's middle reads exactly zero current — at that balance point, the unknown resistance can be calculated purely from the three known ones, with no need to precisely calibrate the measuring galvanometer itself at all.
entries.note: Wheatstone, C. (1843). 'An Account of Several New Instruments and Processes for Determining the Constants of a Voltaic Circuit.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, London, popularising a circuit first described by Samuel Hunter Christie in 1833. Wheatstone openly credited Christie's earlier work and never claimed to have invented the bridge himself, though his name became permanently attached to it through his effective promotion and refinement of the technique.

entries.label: The Michelson Interferometer
entries.hint: An interferometer splits a single beam of light into two paths, sends them along different routes, then recombines them — any difference in the two paths' length, down to a small fraction of the light's own wavelength, shows up as a shift in the resulting interference pattern. Albert Michelson used the technique to redefine the metre itself in terms of a specific, exactly reproducible wavelength of light, rather than a single physical bar of metal that could be damaged, lost, or subtly change size over time.
entries.note: Michelson, A.A. (1893). Measurements conducted at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, Sèvres, near Paris, redefining the metre as a specific number of wavelengths of cadmium red light. Michelson had built the same basic interferometer design over a decade earlier for a quite different purpose — attempting to detect Earth's motion through a hypothesised luminiferous ether — work covered in the quantum-nuclear-relativity folio; the instrument itself became one of the most widely used precision measurement tools in physics regardless of that experiment's outcome.

entries.label: Diffraction Grating Spectroscopy
entries.hint: A diffraction grating — a surface ruled with thousands of closely, precisely spaced parallel lines — splits light into its component wavelengths far more sharply and measurably than a simple prism, since each wavelength diffracts at its own distinct, calculable angle. The technique turned spectroscopy from a qualitative art of comparing colours by eye into a precise measurement science capable of pinning down wavelengths to fractions of a nanometre.
entries.note: Fraunhofer, J. von (1821). 'Neue Modifikation des Lichtes durch gegenseitige Einwirkung und Beugung der Strahlen.' Denkschriften der Königlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu München, at his optical workshop in Munich, where Fraunhofer ruled gratings using a precision dividing engine of his own design. Modern diffraction gratings, ruled or holographically produced with thousands of lines per millimetre, remain the core dispersive element in essentially every research-grade spectrometer built since.

entries.label: The Method of Images
entries.hint: Some electrostatics problems involving charges near a conducting surface — a charge near a flat grounded plate, or near a grounded sphere — can be solved exactly by replacing the awkward conducting boundary with a cleverly placed fictitious 'image' charge on the far side, chosen so its field exactly reproduces the boundary's real effect, then simply calculating the field from the real and image charges together as if the boundary weren't there at all.
entries.note: Thomson, W. [Lord Kelvin] (1848). 'Extraits de deux lettres adressées à M. Liouville.' Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées, written at the University of Glasgow and communicated to the Paris mathematician Joseph Liouville. The technique reduces certain problems that would otherwise require solving a difficult partial differential equation (Laplace's equation) with awkward boundary conditions into simple, direct algebra, and remains a standard textbook tool in electromagnetism courses.

entries.label: Polarimetry
entries.hint: Certain substances, including many sugars and other biologically important molecules, rotate the plane of polarised light passing through them by an amount proportional to the substance's concentration — letting a polarimeter measure a solution's concentration purely optically, by the angle of rotation, with no chemical reaction or destructive testing required.
entries.note: Biot, J.B. (1815). 'Phénomènes de polarisation successive, observés dans des fluides homogènes.' Bulletin des Sciences par la Société Philomathique de Paris, at the Collège de France. The technique became commercially indispensable to the nineteenth-century sugar industry for rapidly and non-destructively grading raw sugar purity, and the underlying molecular property it detects — chirality, a molecule's 'handedness' — is now recognised as fundamental to biochemistry and pharmacology, since a chiral drug's two mirror-image forms can have entirely different biological effects.

entries.label: The Galvanometer
entries.hint: Ørsted had shown a compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire, but the effect was faint; Johann Schweigger's insight was to wind the wire into a multi-turn coil around the compass needle, so each loop's magnetic field added to the others, multiplying the deflection many times over and turning a barely visible curiosity into a genuinely usable instrument for detecting and measuring small electric currents.
entries.note: Schweigger, J.S.C. (1820). 'Elektromagnetischer Multiplicator.' Journal für Chemie und Physik, at the University of Halle, built within months of Ørsted's discovery (see st3). Refined galvanometer designs remained the standard method for measuring electric current for over a century, directly enabling Ohm's precision resistance measurements (see th2) and countless subsequent experiments across electromagnetism.

categories.label: Pioneers & Theorists
categories.subtitle: The researchers who shaped the discipline

entries.label: Benjamin Franklin
entries.hint: Beyond his political career, Franklin was one of the eighteenth century's most respected electrical researchers, coining the terms 'positive' and 'negative' charge, 'battery,' and 'conductor' still used today, and proposing the (as it turned out, arbitrary and now permanently backward) convention for which type of charge counts as 'positive' — a choice later revealed by electron discovery to have picked the direction opposite to how electrons actually flow.
entries.note: Franklin, B. Kite experiment (1752, see st1); also inventor of the lightning rod, a practical application of his electrical theories that spread across Europe and America within his own lifetime. Franklin's single-fluid theory of electricity — that electrical phenomena involve one substance moving between objects, rather than two opposing fluids as some contemporaries proposed — proved substantially correct in spirit, decades before anyone knew what that 'fluid' actually was at the atomic level.

entries.label: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb
entries.hint: A military engineer by training, Coulomb built an extraordinarily sensitive torsion balance capable of detecting forces thousands of times weaker than the instruments of his contemporaries could measure, and used it to establish the precise inverse-square law now bearing his name — the electrical counterpart to Newton's law of gravitation, discovered over a century after Newton's original.
entries.note: Coulomb, C.A. de. 'Premier mémoire sur l'électricité et le magnétisme' (1785, see th1). Coulomb also made major contributions to structural and soil mechanics engineering earlier in his career, including foundational work on friction and the strength of materials, before turning to electricity and magnetism relatively late in his working life; the SI unit of electric charge, the coulomb, is named in his honour.

entries.label: Alessandro Volta
entries.hint: Volta's decade-long public dispute with fellow Italian scientist Luigi Galvani over the true source of 'animal electricity' — Galvani insisted it originated in living tissue itself, Volta argued it came from the contact between two different metals — drove Volta to build the voltaic pile specifically to prove his point, inadvertently inventing the world's first battery and settling the debate largely in his own favour along the way.
entries.note: Volta, A. Voltaic pile (1800, see st2). Napoleon Bonaparte, deeply impressed by a demonstration of the pile, made Volta a count and senator of the Kingdom of Italy; the volt, the SI unit of electric potential, is named in his honour, one of the relatively few electrical units named for someone who was unambiguously the sole inventor of the device that made the unit relevant.

entries.label: Hans Christian Ørsted
entries.hint: A Danish physicist and chemist steeped in the Romantic-era philosophical conviction that all of nature's forces must be fundamentally unified, Ørsted had been actively searching for a connection between electricity and magnetism for years before he finally observed one directly during a lecture demonstration — a discovery that instantly triggered a continent-wide race to work out the mathematical relationship.
entries.note: Ørsted, H.C. Discovery of electromagnetism (1820, see st3). Ørsted also isolated aluminium in a relatively impure form in 1825, predating Hans Christian Ørsted's better-known electromagnetic work in the popular imagination but generally considered less significant scientifically; the SI unit of magnetic field strength in the older CGS system, the oersted, is named in his honour.

entries.label: André-Marie Ampère
entries.hint: Largely self-taught after his father was guillotined during the French Revolution's Reign of Terror, Ampère moved with extraordinary speed once news of Ørsted's discovery reached him, developing a full mathematical theory of electrodynamics within weeks and coining the terms 'electric current' and 'electrodynamics' still in standard use today.
entries.note: Ampère, A.M. 'Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électrodynamiques' (1826, see th3). Maxwell later called Ampère 'the Newton of electricity' in tribute to the mathematical rigour he brought to the field; the SI unit of electric current, the ampere, is named in his honour, and remains one of the seven SI base units.

entries.label: Michael Faraday
entries.hint: Born into poverty and apprenticed to a bookbinder with almost no formal education, Faraday became arguably the greatest experimental physicist in history through sheer relentless curiosity, discovering electromagnetic induction, the laws of electrolysis, and diamagnetism, and originating the physical field concept — all while remaining, by his own repeated choice, largely innocent of the advanced mathematics his own discoveries would eventually require.
entries.note: Faraday, M. Induction ring experiment (1831, see st4); field concept (1852, see co1). Faraday twice declined the presidency of the Royal Society and reportedly refused a knighthood, preferring, on religious grounds tied to his Sandemanian faith, to remain 'plain Michael Faraday to the last'; the SI unit of capacitance, the farad, is named in his honour.

entries.label: Georg Simon Ohm
entries.hint: Working in relative obscurity as a secondary-school teacher with limited laboratory resources, Ohm derived and experimentally confirmed the precise mathematical relationship between voltage, current, and resistance that now bears his name, only to see the work initially dismissed by Germany's physics establishment as unrigorous speculation rather than the rigorous quantitative achievement it actually was.
entries.note: Ohm, G.S. Die galvanische Kette (1827, see th2). Ohm was reportedly so discouraged by his work's poor early reception that he resigned his teaching post; recognition came slowly but eventually thoroughly, including the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1841 and, finally, a professorship at the University of Munich in 1852, four years before his death. The SI unit of electrical resistance, the ohm, is named in his honour.

entries.label: Heinrich Hertz
entries.hint: Hertz's experimental confirmation of Maxwell's predicted electromagnetic waves settled, within a single research program, one of the biggest open theoretical questions in nineteenth-century physics — yet Hertz himself, dead of blood poisoning at just 36, never lived to see the explosion of practical radio technology his discovery directly enabled within barely a decade of his death.
entries.note: Hertz, H. 'Über sehr schnelle electrische Schwingungen' (1887–88, see st5). The SI unit of frequency, the hertz — cycles per second — is named in his honour, adopted internationally in 1960, replacing the earlier unit name 'cycles per second' directly; Hertz's early death from a chronic illness likely related to an untreated bone infection cut short what colleagues widely expected would have been an exceptionally distinguished career.

entries.label: Thomas Young
entries.hint: A physician by profession and one of the last people to plausibly claim expertise across virtually the entire scope of contemporary science, Young's double-slit interference experiment single-handedly revived the wave theory of light against a century of Newtonian orthodoxy, while he separately made major contributions to the study of vision, elasticity, and — completely outside physics — the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphics on the Rosetta Stone.
entries.note: Young, T. 'The Bakerian Lecture: Experiments and Calculations Relative to Physical Optics' (1804, see st9). Young faced sustained, sometimes personally vicious criticism for reviving a theory then considered thoroughly refuted by Newton's authority; his own scientific reputation was robust enough to survive the attacks relatively intact, and Fresnel's later independent confirmation (see st10) fully vindicated his position within his own lifetime.

entries.label: Augustin-Jean Fresnel
entries.hint: A civil engineer by day, building roads and bridges for the French government, Fresnel developed his rigorous mathematical wave theory of light largely in his spare time, without a university research position, and lived to see his theory's most startling and initially ridiculed prediction — a bright spot at the centre of a disc's shadow — experimentally confirmed exactly as his mathematics demanded.
entries.note: Fresnel, A.J. 'Mémoire sur la diffraction de la lumière' (1818, see st10). Fresnel died of tuberculosis at just 39, having also invented the Fresnel lens — a lightweight, thin, stepped lens design still used in lighthouses and, much later, stage lighting and vehicle headlights — which he developed specifically to make lighthouse beams far more powerful and visible from greater distances than traditional solid glass lenses allowed.

entries.label: Ibn al-Haytham
entries.hint: Reportedly held under house arrest in Cairo for roughly a decade after failing to deliver on a boastful promise to the Fatimid Caliph to regulate the flooding of the Nile, Ibn al-Haytham used the enforced isolation to write his monumental Book of Optics, refuting a thousand years of Greek assumptions about vision and establishing controlled, repeatable experiment as the proper foundation for physical theory.
entries.note: Ibn al-Haytham [Alhazen]. Kitāb al-Manāẓir (c. 1021, see st7). Some historical accounts suggest Ibn al-Haytham feigned madness during his house arrest as a survival strategy under the notoriously unpredictable Caliph al-Hakim, only resuming a normal public life after the Caliph's death in 1021; regardless of the exact biographical details, which vary somewhat between historical sources, his experimental methodology's influence on the later European scientific tradition, via Latin translation, is well documented.

entries.label: Joseph von Fraunhofer
entries.hint: Orphaned at eleven and apprenticed to a brutal glassmaker whose workshop collapsed and nearly killed him — a disaster that, in a stroke of fortune, brought him to the attention of the Bavarian royal family, who funded his education — Fraunhofer went on to become the finest optical instrument maker of his generation, discovering the dark spectral lines that now bear his name almost as a side effect of his real goal: making better glass.
entries.note: Fraunhofer, J. von. Discovery of solar absorption lines (1814–15, see co7); diffraction grating spectroscopy (1821, see me3). Fraunhofer's precise refractive index measurements and grating-ruling techniques made his Munich workshop's telescope and microscope lenses the best available anywhere in Europe, and his early death from tuberculosis-related illness at 39, likely worsened by heavy metal exposure during decades of glassmaking, cut short a career already recognised as exceptional.

entries.label: Wilhelm Röntgen
entries.hint: Röntgen's discovery of X-rays came from an unusually thorough, methodical follow-up on a faint, easily-dismissed observation that other researchers using similar cathode ray equipment had likely also noticed and overlooked; his careful week of follow-up experiments, conducted in near-total secrecy before publication, turned a fluorescent screen's faint unexplained glow into one of the most immediately consequential discoveries in the history of medicine.
entries.note: Röntgen, W.C. 'Über eine neue Art von Strahlen' (1895, see st11). Röntgen became the first ever recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and, unusually for the era, donated the entire prize money to his university; he deliberately declined to patent the X-ray or profit financially from it in any way, a decision he maintained was simply the correct one for a discovery of this kind to belong to everyone.

categories.label: Debates & Open Questions
categories.subtitle: Live controversies — where the field is actively contesting the evidence

entries.label: Wave vs. Particle Theory of Light
entries.hint: Newton argued light consists of a stream of tiny particles ('corpuscles') travelling in straight lines, while Huygens argued it was a wave propagating through a medium; Newton's immense scientific authority kept the corpuscular view dominant for over a century, until Young's interference pattern and Fresnel's diffraction mathematics made the wave picture's predictive superiority essentially impossible to deny.
entries.note: Newton, I. (1704). Opticks. London: Royal Society, the corpuscular theory's most influential statement. The debate did not stay settled forever: twentieth-century quantum mechanics revealed light genuinely exhibits both wave and particle behaviour depending on how it's measured, a resolution neither seventeenth-century camp could have anticipated and one covered in full in the quantum-nuclear-relativity folio.

entries.label: Action at a Distance vs. Field Theory
entries.hint: Continental physicists including Wilhelm Weber and Franz Neumann built successful electrodynamic theories treating electric and magnetic forces as acting instantaneously across empty space, directly between distant charges, with no mediating substance in between; Faraday insisted instead that space itself, filled with field lines, was doing the physical work, a view most of his contemporaries considered an unnecessary and unverifiable philosophical addition until Maxwell's equations made the field picture mathematically indispensable.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1846). 'Thoughts on Ray Vibrations.' Philosophical Magazine, 28, 345–350, at the Royal Institution, London — Faraday's explicit early argument that a mediating field, not instantaneous action, must be responsible. Maxwell's equations (see th6) require a finite propagation speed for electromagnetic effects, matching the field picture and directly contradicting instantaneous action at a distance; the debate is now considered settled decisively in the field theory's favour.

entries.label: Does the Luminiferous Ether Exist?
entries.hint: If light is a wave, as Maxwell's theory required, nineteenth-century physicists reasoned it needed some physical medium to wave in — an invisible, weightless, perfectly rigid-yet-frictionless 'luminiferous ether' filling all of space — and Maxwell himself proposed specific experiments that might detect Earth's motion through this hypothesised medium.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. (1878). 'Ether.' Encyclopaedia Britannica, 9th ed., written at Cambridge, proposing methods to detect ether drift that directly motivated Michelson's later experiments. The question was decisively resolved by the Michelson-Morley experiment's null result and Einstein's subsequent special relativity, which dispensed with the ether concept entirely — both covered in full in the quantum-nuclear-relativity folio.

entries.label: Transverse vs. Longitudinal Light Waves
entries.hint: If light waves vibrate along their direction of travel, like sound, polarisation makes no sense at all — but if they vibrate side to side, transversely, the medium carrying them would seemingly need to be an impossibly rigid, almost solid-like substance to support that kind of vibration, while somehow still letting planets move through it without any detectable resistance whatsoever.
entries.note: Fresnel, A.J. Letter to André-Marie Ampère, 1821, Paris, first clearly proposing transverse light waves to explain polarisation despite the apparent mechanical absurdity involved. The 'rigid ether' problem the transverse hypothesis created was never fully solved within classical physics on its own terms; it was ultimately dissolved rather than answered, once Maxwell's field theory (see th6) removed the need for any material medium for light to travel through at all.

entries.label: AC vs. DC: The War of the Currents
entries.hint: Thomas Edison championed direct current for the emerging electrical grid, while George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla backed alternating current, which transformers could step up to high voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and back down for safe local use — a decisive practical advantage direct current, without an equivalent transformer technology, simply couldn't match at the time.
entries.note: The dispute peaked publicly around 1888, including a well-documented Edison-backed public relations campaign emphasising AC's electrocution dangers, notoriously including electrocuting animals to make the point. Westinghouse's AC system's selection to power the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, and Niagara Falls' hydroelectric AC generating station shortly after, effectively settled the commercial contest in AC's favour, though DC remains standard for many modern applications including battery-powered electronics and long-distance high-voltage transmission lines.

entries.label: Can Radio Waves Follow Earth's Curvature?
entries.hint: Radio waves, like light, should travel in straight lines — meaning a signal transmitted from one side of the Atlantic should be physically blocked by the curve of the Earth long before reaching the other side, according to the straightforward geometry involved. Marconi's transatlantic transmission succeeded anyway, leaving physicists to work out exactly why, a puzzle not fully resolved until the ionosphere's reflective properties were confirmed over two decades later.
entries.note: Marconi, G. (1901). Transatlantic radio transmission, Poldhu, Cornwall to St. John's, Newfoundland, widely reported at the time though some contemporaries doubted whether the signal had genuinely been received as claimed, given the lack of independent verification. Oliver Heaviside and Arthur Kennelly independently proposed a reflecting atmospheric layer the same year to explain the result theoretically; Appleton's 1924 experiments (see ef9) finally confirmed the layer directly.

entries.label: Do Power Lines Pose a Health Risk?
entries.hint: A widely publicised epidemiological study suggested children living near high-voltage power lines had elevated rates of leukaemia, raising public alarm over the low-frequency electric and magnetic fields such lines produce — despite no known physical mechanism by which such weak, non-ionising fields could plausibly damage DNA the way higher-energy ionising radiation does.
entries.note: Wertheimer, N. & Leeper, E. (1979). 'Electrical Wiring Configurations and Childhood Cancer.' American Journal of Epidemiology, 109(3), 273–284, Denver, Colorado. Subsequent, much larger and more rigorous studies, along with reviews by major health bodies including the World Health Organization, have found no convincing established causal link, and the original study's exposure-classification methodology has been specifically criticised; public concern nonetheless persists, and some countries maintain precautionary exposure guidelines despite the absence of confirmed mechanism or robustly replicated effect.

entries.label: Who Really Invented Radio: Marconi or Tesla?
entries.hint: Guglielmo Marconi is popularly credited as radio's inventor and won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics for it, but Nikola Tesla had filed several of the foundational radio-related patents years earlier — a dispute that dragged through patent courts for decades and was only resolved, in Tesla's favour on some key points, by a Supreme Court ruling handed down after both men were already dead.
entries.note: US Supreme Court, Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States (1943), invalidating several of Marconi's key patents by citing prior work by Tesla, Oliver Lodge, and John Stone Stone. The ruling was decided on narrow patent-law grounds relating to a wartime government dispute, not as any comprehensive historical judgment about scientific priority, and popular credit for radio's invention has remained genuinely contested and nationally inflected ever since — celebrated as Marconi in much of the English-speaking world and as Tesla in much of Eastern Europe and Serbia specifically.

categories.label: Applications
categories.subtitle: Where the science leaves the lab

entries.label: The Electric Motor & Generator
entries.hint: Faraday demonstrated a wire carrying current continuously rotating around a fixed magnet — the first device ever to convert electrical energy directly into sustained mechanical motion, rather than a single brief jolt. The same basic principle, run in reverse, converts mechanical motion into electrical current, and together the two directions underlie virtually every electric motor and generator built since.
entries.note: Faraday, M. (1821). 'On Some New Electro-Magnetical Motions, and on the Theory of Magnetism.' Quarterly Journal of Science, 12, 74–96, at the Royal Institution, London — the earliest demonstration of continuous electromagnetic rotation, a full decade before Faraday's induction discovery (see st4, th4) put the underlying relationship on a rigorous theoretical footing. Practical, commercially viable electric motors and generators took several more decades of engineering refinement to develop into genuinely useful machines.

entries.label: The Electric Telegraph
entries.hint: The electric telegraph sent messages by opening and closing a circuit in patterns that deflected needles or clicked a receiver at the far end of a wire, letting information travel at nearly the speed of electricity itself rather than at the speed of a horse, ship, or train — the first technology in history to fundamentally decouple long-distance communication speed from physical transportation speed.
entries.note: Cooke, W.F. & Wheatstone, C. (1837). British Patent No. 7390, 'Improvements in Giving Signals and Sounding Alarums in Distant Places by Means of Electric Currents,' London, developed by the same Wheatstone who later popularised the resistance-measuring bridge (see me1). Samuel Morse independently developed a competing telegraph system in the United States the same year; the telegraph network's rapid nineteenth-century expansion is often described by historians as the 'Victorian Internet' for its transformative effect on the speed of global communication and commerce.

entries.label: Fiber Optics
entries.hint: A hair-thin strand of extremely pure glass can carry a light signal for many kilometres via continuous total internal reflection off its own inner surface, bouncing the light down the fibre's length with remarkably little loss — turning a phenomenon first demonstrated as a parlour trick with a curved stream of water into the physical infrastructure carrying the overwhelming majority of the world's long-distance internet and telephone traffic.
entries.note: Kao, C.K. & Hockham, G.A. (1966). 'Dielectric-Fibre Surface Waveguides for Optical Frequencies.' Proceedings of the IEE, 113(7), 1151–1158, at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories, Harlow, England, showing existing fibre losses were due to impurities rather than any fundamental physical limit, and that sufficiently pure glass could transmit light over genuinely useful distances. Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work; modern undersea fibre-optic cables now carry the vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic.

entries.label: Radio & Wireless Communication
entries.hint: Barely more than a decade after Hertz demonstrated electromagnetic waves in his laboratory as a purely scientific curiosity of no obvious practical use, Guglielmo Marconi had turned the same physics into a working transatlantic communication system, transmitting the letter 'S' in Morse code across the Atlantic Ocean with no wire connection at all — arguably the fastest translation from pure scientific discovery to world-changing technology in the whole history of physics up to that point.
entries.note: Marconi, G. (1901). Transatlantic radio transmission, Poldhu, Cornwall to St. John's, Newfoundland, whether radio waves could plausibly follow Earth's curve to make the transmission possible at all was a genuine, unresolved scientific puzzle at the time (see db6). Radio rapidly transformed maritime safety (ship-to-shore distress signalling, prominently including the 1912 Titanic disaster), news distribution, and, within a few more decades, mass entertainment broadcasting.

entries.label: The Laser
entries.hint: A laser generates light that is coherent, monochromatic, and tightly directional to a degree no ordinary light source can match, by stimulating a large population of excited atoms to release photons of exactly matching wavelength and phase all at once — turning the abstract concept of coherence (see co6) into an engineered, controllable, everyday technology used in everything from barcode scanners and fibre-optic communication to surgery and industrial cutting.
entries.note: Maiman, T.H. (1960). 'Stimulated Optical Radiation in Ruby.' Nature, 187, 493–494, at Hughes Research Laboratories, Malibu, California — the first working laser, built using a ruby crystal, months after Maiman's own employer's public relations department had initially downplayed the result's significance. Charles Townes and Arthur Schawlow had laid the theoretical groundwork in a 1958 paper, and the underlying stimulated-emission physics traces back to Einstein's 1917 theoretical work, though Einstein could not have anticipated the eventual device.

entries.label: Medical X-ray Imaging
entries.hint: Within weeks of Röntgen's discovery, doctors were already using X-rays to locate broken bones and embedded objects inside the body without surgery — a medical transformation Marie Curie personally accelerated during the First World War by designing mobile X-ray units, nicknamed 'petites Curies,' and training over a hundred women to operate them at field hospitals near the front lines, helping military surgeons locate bullets and shrapnel directly.
entries.note: Curie, M. (1914–18). Organised approximately 20 mobile radiography vehicles and roughly 200 additional fixed radiological installations across French military hospitals during the First World War, funded substantially through her own Nobel Prize money and public appeals. Modern medical X-ray imaging has since diversified into computed tomography (CT), mammography, and fluoroscopy, but the basic physical principle — differential absorption of X-rays by tissues of different density — remains exactly the one Röntgen first identified in 1895 (see st11).
